# Notes on 1 Kings 8:45–66

**What's missing:** I ran out of search budget and couldn't read the full Enduring Word and Precept Austin pages, because both cut off before these verses. I found nothing on vv. 51–53 and only a little on v. 60. I also found nothing from Catholic or Orthodox sources, from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org, or about prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this passage. The only real split between Protestant traditions I found is at v. 46 (with a smaller one at v. 58).

---

**v. 45**
- Guzik says Solomon asks God to hear prayers for victory only when they battle as God *sent* them. This was not a blanket request for blessing on every military adventure. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/
- Matthew Henry: Soldiers in the field must not think it enough that those who tarry at home pray for them, but must pray for themselves. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_008.cfm
- Precept Austin: Solomon knew that God is for His people. So Solomon could ask God to help them in wartime. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-8-commentary

**v. 46 ("there is no one who does not sin"): where the traditions differ**
- *Reformed and Calvinist readers:* Gill explains it by the depravity of human nature, the treachery of the heart, and the temptations of Satan, and links it to Ecclesiastes 7:20. https://pro.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-46.html Henry says there is no man but what is in danger of falling into gross sin, and will if God leave him to himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-46.html Poole reads it as a forecast that Israel will sin, and also as a reason to hope God won't deal with them as their sins deserve. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-46.htm A modern Bible Hub study note says the line underscores the doctrine of original sin. https://biblehub.com/study/1_kings/8-46.htm
- *Methodist and Wesleyan readers:* Adam Clarke says the Hebrew should read "no man that *may* not sin," meaning there is no man *impeccable*, none *infallible*, none that is not *liable* to transgress. He notes the verse has been a wonderful strong hold for all who believe that there is no redemption from sin in this life, but replies that it only speaks of the possibility of every man sinning. He calls the opposite view a dangerous and destructive doctrine. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-kings-8.html Whedon agrees that the point is no man, and no nation, that can claim to be beyond the possibility of sinning. He adds that the verse doesn't prove a New Testament believer must sin every hour. https://pro.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-46.html Benson (also Methodist) says the words do not contradict the declaration of St. John, that he who is born of God, sinneth not. https://pro.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-46.html
- *Churches of Christ:* Coffman: "The idea of total hereditary depravity is not supported in the Bible, but it is nevertheless an observed and undeniable fact that all men are sinners. https://beta.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-46.html
- *Background:* the Cambridge Bible says these verses should be compared with Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-46.htm Precept Austin notes that Only one that ever walked this earth was holy, guileless, and undefiled, Hebrews 7:26. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-8-commentary

**v. 47**
- The Pulpit and Keil notes on Bible Hub say the Hebrew phrase means "they take it to heart" (compare Deuteronomy 4:39 and 30:1), not merely that they feel remorse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-46.htm
- Coffman sees three words for sin in this verse: missing the goal, deliberate iniquity, and abnormal wickedness. https://beta.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-46.html
- Bible Hub cross-references Daniel 9:5, "we have sinned and done wrong." https://biblehub.com/1_kings/8-46.htm

**v. 48**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Solomon prays for their restoration only in the event of their returning unto the Lord with all their heart, and with all their soul. https://pro.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-46.html Coffman likewise says forgiveness depending on the sinner's turning away from his transgressions is a major thesis of the prayer. https://beta.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-46.html
- On praying "toward" the land: a writer quoted at Precept Austin says the phrase assures God's people that they do not have to be *at or in* the temple to be heard. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-8-commentary Guzik says this shows God's reach extends beyond the physical building. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

**vv. 49–50**
- Precept Austin: Solomon knew that God hates sin and yet loves the sinner (1Ki 8:46–51). So Solomon could ask, no matter how great the sin or how terrible the discipline, that when God's people returned to Him the Lord would forgive and restore their fortunes. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-8-commentary
- Bible Hub links this to Jeremiah 29 and Nehemiah 1. It says the same God who judges is ready to restore any heart that turns back to Him. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/8-46.htm

**v. 54**
- Henry calls the posture very reverent, and expressive of humility, seriousness, and fervency in prayer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_008.cfm
- An older commentary on the Bible Hub v. 58 page points out that the consecration was done not by the high priest or any member of the Aaronic family, but by the king in person. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-58.htm Guzik explains that Solomon stayed outside the sanctuary because he was a king and not a priest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

**v. 55**
- Henry: Having spoken to God for them, he here speaks from God to them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_008.cfm

**v. 56**
- Henry notices that God is praised for giving *rest*, not wealth or power, as if that were a blessing more valuable than any of those. He calls "not one word has failed" a receipt in full on the back of these bonds. He also looks ahead to the day God's spiritual Israel will rest from their labours. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_008.cfm
- Keil says the rest given under Joshua was only fully secured by David's victories. That fulfilment gave hope for the promises to David, if the people themselves would only faithfully adhere to their God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-58.htm
- Precept Austin links this to the "rest" of Hebrews 4. It quotes a writer who says His precepts are our rule; promises are his responsibility. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-8-commentary

**v. 57**
- G. Campbell Morgan says God's presence depended on the people's obedience, but Solomon saw that their obedience was dependent on His presence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gcm/1-kings-8.html?print=yes

**v. 58 ("may He incline our hearts"): differences in emphasis**
- *Reformed:* the Geneva note says Solomon concludes that man of himself is enemy to God, and that all obedience to his law proceeds from his mercy. Gill says God inclines hearts By his Spirit, to love, fear, and serve him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-58.htm Henry: Our hearts are naturally averse to our duty, and apt to decline from God; it is his grace that inclines them, grace that must be obtained by prayer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_008.cfm
- *Anglican:* Ellicott reads v. 58 together with v. 61 as showing the true, though mysterious, co-operation of the "preventing grace" of God with man's free responsibility. In short, God "inclines the heart" and yet the heart must yield itself. He points to Philippians 2:12–13. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-58.htm
- *Methodist:* Benson asks that God by his Holy Spirit, effectually incline us to obey it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-58.htm
- *Devotional:* Precept Austin quotes a writer who says God will never compel us to be good and obedient—but He will incline us, persuade us, draw us, help us. Its own note says Fallen flesh cannot if left to itself incline, walk or keep! https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-8-commentary
- Barnes says this teaching first appears in Scripture in the Davidical Psalms. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-58.htm

**v. 59**
- Henry sees a picture of Christ here: the prayer is still granted in the intercession of Christ, of which his supplication was a type. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-58.html
- Precept Austin points to the Revised Version margin for "as each day requires": "the thing of a day in its day." Whatever may be the requirement for any day, the abundance of grace needed is provided. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64362/

**v. 60**
- The only note I found is a writer quoted at Precept Austin. He says God's grace alone could incline their hearts (v. 58) and enable them to glorify their God in the world, verse 60. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-8-commentary

**v. 61**
- Henry: He solemnly charges his people to continue and persevere in their duty to God. He adds that those only would fare the better for his prayers that were made better by his preaching. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_008.cfm
- Henry's Concise Commentary: No human heart is of itself willing to obey the gospel call, yet Solomon still urges the people to be perfect. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-58.htm

**vv. 62–63**
- Benson and Poole say the animals were offered Not all in one day, but in seven, or, it may be, in the fourteen days. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-63.htm Clarke counts them as the total for all fourteen days. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-kings-8.html
- The Cambridge Bible notes that peace offerings were mostly eaten, which explains in part the enormous number of animals. It also records that Josephus gives 12,000 oxen rather than 22,000. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-63.htm
- Keil works out the logistics against the doubts of Thenius. He argues there was no difficulty in slaughtering and sacrificing 3000 oxen and 18,000 sheep each day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-63.htm The Pulpit Commentary argues that the numbers include the people's own offerings. It rejects the view that all the victims were offered by Solomon alone (Ewald, Stanley). https://biblehub.com/1_kings/8-63.htm Coffman agrees. https://studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-63.html
- Ellicott accepts the number, but adds a warning. The lavish display may perhaps have involved something of the idea, so frequent in heathen sacrifice, and so emphatically condemned by the prophets. In such ideas lurked the evils which hereafter were to overthrow the prosperity of Israel. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/8-63.htm
- The Bible Hub study note says the scale foreshadows the once-for-all sufficiency of Christ's sacrifice (Hebrews 10:10-12). While Solomon needed tens of thousands, Jesus needed only Himself. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/8-63.htm
- Chuck Smith calls it Probably the biggest barbecue on record. https://studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-63.html

**v. 64**
- Keil: the bronze altar might not have been large enough, because the daily burnt offerings had to be added as well. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-63.htm Constable: Perhaps the priests made sacrifices at other places outside the temple courtyard. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-65.html
- Chuck Smith: they made the whole area holy and they offered up the burned offerings all over the courtyard. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-65.html

**v. 65**
- *Boundaries:* the phrase means "from one extremity of the land to the other." Ellicott says the Brook of Egypt is not the Nile but the stream at El-Arish. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-65.htm
- *"Seven days and seven more days":* most read this as seven days of dedication followed by seven days of the Feast of Tabernacles. JFB adds that the fourteen days were not continuous, because the Day of Atonement fell in between. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Ki/1Ki_008.cfm Keil places the dedication on days 8–14 and Tabernacles on days 15–21. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-65.htm In contrast, Coffman reports that La Sor took the two feasts as running concurrently, or simultaneously. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-65.html
- *Text:* Gill notes that the Vatican copy of the Septuagint says "seven days" only once. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-65.htm The NRSV likewise reads only "seven days." https://biblehub.com/1_kings/8-65.htm
- *Application:* Henry notes that the people kept fourteen days of worship, yet they said not, *Behold, what a weariness is this!* https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-65.html William Kelly sees a picture of the great gathering of the latter day under Christ, the true Son of David. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/8-65.html

**v. 66**
These are my own summaries of the page. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/8-66.htm
- Where the BSB has "fifteenth day," older translations say "eighth day." The Cambridge Bible and the Pulpit Commentary take it as the eighth day of Tabernacles, which is the fifteenth day of the whole celebration.
- Keil squares this with 2 Chronicles 7:10 ("the twenty-third day"). He says Solomon dismissed the people on the evening of the 22nd, and they set off home the next morning.
- Barnes and Pulpit: going home "to their tents" is an old phrase left over from Israel's tent-dwelling days.
- Poole: "blessed the king" means they prayed for him or thanked him.
- Pulpit: David is named because he was the real founder of the temple. Keil adds that the temple fulfilled God's promise to David.
- Henry's Concise Commentary: we too should go home rejoicing from worship.
